domain_label: Knowledge-Graph Architect — Graph Schema & Structure (typed nodes/edges, prerequisite DAG, hub detection, flat-spine→full-graph graduation)
purpose: How a knowledge-graph architect turns contenteng's flat edge table into a real, typed knowledge graph over the app's Concept and ConceptEdge entities — fixing the node schema, the closed relation vocabulary and edge directionality, the prerequisite DAG and part_of hierarchy, hub-node detection, the integrity invariants, and the honest decision of when to graduate from a flat ordered spine to a full graph — kept honest by grounding the edge=(A,relation,B) proposition in contenteng's already-in-repo kb_book_decomposition and every app-entity fact in APP_RECON.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all base scores are heuristic priors and every structural-design call is an ESTIMATE synthesized from the cited grounding files

the edge=(A,relation,B) proposition definition, the Novak & Canas 2008 concept-map framing and the Doignon & Falmagne 1985 Knowledge Space Theory surmise relation are inherited as-is from contenteng kb_book_decomposition (already in-repo) and are cited to it rather than re-derived
the app's Concept and ConceptEdge entities are the fixed persistence target: node/edge schema decisions must map onto their existing fields per APP_RECON, not invent a new store

this KB is the SCHEMA & STRUCTURE third of the kgraph specialist; medical/dental terminology linking (term recognition, synonym normalization, hover-definition attachment) and the graph-view rendering are neighboring KBs this one only hands off to
exclusions: terminology linking — recognizing a term in card text, normalizing synonyms, attaching the definition a hover shows (a separate kgraph KB) beyond emitting the typed node a term resolves to
the visual encoding, layout, semantic zoom and color system of the graph view (owned by the viz specialist) beyond naming node type and hub degree as encodable attributes
the contenteng book->units->terms->claims->relations->cards decomposition pipeline and its card-quality/coverage gate beyond consuming its edge table as the graph's raw material
the learner-model scheduling and adaptive item-selection algorithms (BKT/Elo/FSRS, owned by learner/sched) beyond exposing the prereq DAG and hub structure they would consume
building the missing ConceptEdge writer, the graph library, or the scheduled pipeline in the app (owned by extint/app engineering) beyond specifying the schema and invariants such code must honor

glossary.definition: A graph whose vertices are typed entity nodes (here Concepts) and whose arcs are typed relations drawn from a closed vocabulary, carrying enough structure (direction, transitivity, acyclicity of the prereq layer) to be queried and traversed for learning-path and hub reasoning — the object contenteng's flat edge table is graduated into.

The atomic unit of the graph: a triple of a source concept A, a relation, and a target concept B, identical to the concept-map proposition of Novak & Canas 2008; inherited from contenteng kb_book_decomposition, where the equation edges~=propositions is carried as the owner's-term [ESTIMATE].

The app's persisted node: a Concept row with exam_code and name (required), plus bloom level and the INBDE blueprint axes inbde_fk (1-10), inbde_cc (1-56), inbde_cc_section (DTP/OHM/PP) and toefl_section (R/L/S/W) [FACT-source: APP_RECON, Concept.jsonc].

The app's persisted edge: a ConceptEdge row with src_concept_id, dst_concept_id and type in {prereq, related, part_of} (default prereq); read once by runPipeline's prerequisite check but written by no code in the shipped repo [FACT-source: APP_RECON section 5.5, 4a].

The subgraph of prereq edges, which must be a directed acyclic graph so a topological ordering (a valid learning sequence) exists; the graph realization of the Knowledge Space Theory surmise relation.

Doignon & Falmagne 1985: a prerequisite ordering over items whose acyclic structure constrains the reachable knowledge states and learning paths, with the fringe (items one step ahead) having maximal diagnostic value; inherited from contenteng, deployed commercially in ALEKS [FACT-source: contenteng kb_book_decomposition].

A node with high degree centrality — many incident edges — which contenteng flags via heavily-indexed terms; pedagogically a high-connectivity, high-yield concept whose mastery unlocks or supports many others, so it is taught early and weighted heavily.

The simplest structure: concepts in a single linear order (chapter/unit order) that approximates prerequisites without explicit edges — contenteng's Option F, cheap to author and to schedule against, but unable to express branching prerequisite structure.

A graph representation where both nodes and edges are first-class objects carrying a type label and attribute key-values (as opposed to RDF's uniform subject-predicate-object triples), the model that fits the app's Concept/ConceptEdge row-per-object store.

The containment structure formed by part_of edges — a directed, transitive aggregation of concepts into larger units — mapping onto the app's roll-up of concepts into INBDE FK areas and CC sections used by the mastery report.

nodes.definition: Frame the architect's task: contenteng emits a flat edge table (term_a, relation, term_b, unit_id) and deliberately stops there, deferring a full knowledge graph until adaptive selection demands it [FACT-source: contenteng kb_book_decomposition; APP_RECON KG deferral]. This KB graduates that table into a real, TYPED knowledge graph over the app's Concept/ConceptEdge entities: typed entity nodes, typed directed relations, an acyclic prerequisite layer, a part_of containment hierarchy and detectable hub nodes, so the structure can be queried for learning paths, high-yield concepts and prerequisite gates rather than just listed. The payoff over the raw table is queryable STRUCTURE (reachability, topological order, centrality); the cost is the schema discipline and integrity invariants the rest of this KB specifies [ESTIMATE — design synthesis, high confidence].

nodes.definition: Fix the most basic knowledge-representation distinction, because it drives the whole schema: a knowledge graph separates ENTITIES (things — here concepts/terms, which become nodes) from RELATIONS (how two entities stand to each other, which become edges) [ESTIMATE — standard KR/ontology-engineering framing, to source-verify]. A node answers 'what is this thing'; an edge answers 'how does this thing relate to that thing'. The atomic assertion is therefore not a node but an EDGE — a proposition binding two entities by a relation — so meaning lives on the edges while nodes are the anchors they connect. Getting this split right prevents the common error of encoding a relationship as a node attribute (losing traversability) or an entity as an edge label (losing identity).

included: the entity-vs-relation split
nodes-as-anchors, edges-as-assertions
why relationships must be edges not attributes
excluded: the concrete triple grounding (its own node)

pros.claim: Separating entities from relations up front stops relationships being buried as un-traversable node attributes
pros.example: modelling 'A is a prerequisite of B' as a prereq edge rather than a text field on A

cons.claim: The clean split is an idealization; some real knowledge (n-ary relations, qualified statements) resists a plain two-node edge
cons.example: a relation that only holds under a condition needing reification the simple node/edge split omits

failure_modes: encoding a relationship as a node attribute and losing traversal
modelling an entity as an edge label and losing its identity
acceptance_tests: the split names entities-as-nodes and relations-as-edges, states the edge is the atomic assertion, and warns against relationship-as-attribute and entity-as-label errors
revisit_triggers: an n-ary or qualified relation must be modelled

nodes.definition: Ground the atomic edge exactly as contenteng already defines it: an edge is a triple (A, relation, B) — the concept-map PROPOSITION of Novak & Canas 2008 — rendered downstream as a small card family (forward, reverse-if-unique, relation, cloze) [FACT-source: contenteng kb_book_decomposition; the equation edges~=propositions is carried there as the owner's-term ESTIMATE, high confidence]. In the graph, A and B are Concept nodes and the relation is the edge type; the proposition 'periodontal ligament is part_of the periodontium' is one part_of edge. This is the definitional bridge from contenteng's data method to this KB's typed graph: the edge table's rows ARE the graph's edges, so the graph inherits the proposition semantics rather than redefining them.

nodes.definition: Specify the node schema. A node is a distinct CONCEPT identified by a stable id and a human-readable name, carrying a node type and typed attributes; two cards about the same idea must resolve to the SAME node, so node identity (find-or-create by a natural key) is the first invariant [ESTIMATE — design synthesis over the app entity, high confidence]. In the app this is the Concept entity: exam_code and name are required, with bloom level and the INBDE blueprint axes (inbde_fk, inbde_cc, inbde_cc_section) and toefl_section as attributes [FACT-source: APP_RECON, Concept.jsonc]. Nodes are the anchors edges connect, so every node an edge references MUST already exist — node creation strictly precedes edge creation.

node type and typed attributes
nodes-exist-before-edges ordering
excluded: the app field-by-field mapping (its own node)

pros.claim: A stable node identity with find-or-create prevents the same concept splintering into duplicate nodes that fragment the graph
pros.example: two cards on 'gingivitis' resolving to one Concept node instead of two disconnected ones

cons.claim: Natural-key identity is fragile to naming variants, so without synonym normalization near-duplicate nodes still leak in
cons.example: 'MI' and 'myocardial infarction' becoming two nodes until the terminology-linking KB merges them

failure_modes: creating duplicate nodes for one concept
referencing a node from an edge before the node exists
acceptance_tests: the node schema defines identity by stable id + natural-key find-or-create, lists node type and attributes, and states nodes must exist before edges reference them
revisit_triggers: duplicate nodes appear for one concept

nodes.definition: Specify the edge schema. An edge is (src_node, edge_type, dst_node) where edge_type is drawn from a CLOSED relation vocabulary — in the app exactly {prereq, related, part_of} [FACT-source: ConceptEdge.jsonc; APP_RECON]. Each type is a distinct relation with its own directionality and algebra (specified downstream), not an interchangeable label; the type is what makes the edge queryable ('give all prereqs of X' vs 'all parts of X'). Both endpoints must be existing nodes (no dangling edges), and a (src,type,dst) triple is the identity of the edge so duplicates collapse. Keeping the vocabulary CLOSED — a small fixed set rather than free-text relations — is what lets traversal and integrity checks be written once per type.

the closed prereq/related/part_of vocabulary
no-dangling-endpoints and triple-identity dedup

pros.example: a single prereq-DAG check covering every prereq edge because they all share one type

cons.claim: A closed vocabulary cannot express a relation outside the three types without a schema change and a migration
cons.example: a genuine 'contradicts' or 'treats' relation having to be forced into 'related' or deferred

failure_modes: allowing free-text edge types that defeat per-type checks
creating an edge whose endpoints do not both exist
acceptance_tests: the edge schema gives the (src,type,dst) tuple over the closed prereq/related/part_of vocabulary, requires both endpoints to exist, and treats the triple as the edge identity for dedup

nodes.definition: Choose the representation family: a LABELED PROPERTY GRAPH — nodes and edges are first-class objects each carrying a type label and attribute key-values — versus an RDF triple store where everything is uniform subject-predicate-object triples [ESTIMATE — standard KR distinction, to source-verify]. The app already persists a row per Concept and a row per ConceptEdge with typed fields, so it IS a property graph; adopting that model rather than RDF avoids an ontology layer the single-app store does not need. The cost is giving up RDF's formal schema reasoning (OWL inference, SPARQL federation): the property graph gets typed traversal and attribute filtering but not automated logical entailment, which is an acceptable trade at this scale [ESTIMATE, high confidence].

cons.claim: The property graph gives up RDF's formal inference, so entailments must be computed by hand rather than derived

failure_modes: importing RDF/OWL machinery the app does not need

nodes.definition: Govern the relation vocabulary. The three types carry distinct meanings: prereq(A,B) = A must be mastered before B (a learning-order constraint); part_of(A,B) = A is a component/subtopic of the larger unit B (aggregation); related(A,B) = A and B are associatively connected without order or containment (a see-also mesh) [FACT-source: ConceptEdge.jsonc enum; semantics per contenteng KST/concept-map framing]. The vocabulary is closed by design: adding a type is a deliberate schema change with its own directionality, algebra, traversal and invariant, never an ad-hoc string. Overloading 'related' as a dumping ground for anything that is not clearly prereq or part_of is the main degradation risk and must be resisted.

closed-vocabulary governance and how a type is added
the 'related'-as-dumping-ground degradation risk

pros.claim: Precise, disjoint relation meanings keep each edge type queryable for a distinct purpose
pros.example: prereq driving learning order while part_of drives the mastery roll-up, with no overlap

cons.claim: A closed three-type vocabulary forces genuinely different relations into 'related', blurring its meaning over time
cons.example: 'treats', 'causes' and 'contrasts-with' all collapsing into related and losing their distinctions

failure_modes: overloading 'related' with heterogeneous meanings
adding a relation type without defining its algebra and invariants
acceptance_tests: the vocabulary gives disjoint meanings for prereq/part_of/related, states adding a type is a governed schema change, and flags overloading 'related' as the degradation risk
revisit_triggers: 'related' starts absorbing distinct relation meanings

base.update_signal: overloaded 'related' or a repeated new-relation need changes vocabulary governance

nodes.definition: Fix the directionality and algebra of each relation, because traversal correctness depends on it. prereq is DIRECTED and ASYMMETRIC — prereq(A,B) does not imply prereq(B,A), and its transitive closure defines reachable learning states. part_of is DIRECTED and TRANSITIVE — part_of(A,B) and part_of(B,C) imply A is part_of C (containment rolls up). related is SYMMETRIC/UNDIRECTED — related(A,B) is the same fact as related(B,A), so it is stored once and traversed both ways [ESTIMATE — standard relation-algebra, consistent with the KST surmise relation grounding, high confidence]. Mixing these up (treating prereq as symmetric, or related as directed) silently corrupts learning-path and roll-up queries with no error, so each type's direction is a schema-level property, not a per-edge choice.

included: prereq directed/asymmetric
part_of directed/transitive
related symmetric/undirected
why mixing them corrupts traversal

pros.claim: Pinning direction and algebra per type makes traversal queries provably correct and reusable
pros.example: computing prereq reachability by transitive closure knowing prereq never runs backward

cons.claim: Encoding transitivity and symmetry as schema properties means the code, not a reasoner, must honor them everywhere
cons.example: every part_of query having to apply transitive roll-up by hand or miss ancestors

failure_modes: treating prereq as symmetric and inverting learning order
storing related twice or traversing it one-way
acceptance_tests: each type's direction/algebra is stated (prereq directed-asymmetric, part_of directed-transitive, related symmetric) and the traversal-corruption risk of mixing them is named
revisit_triggers: a traversal returns backward or missing relations

base.update_signal: a backward/missing traversal or a new relation changes the directionality rules

nodes.definition: Require the prerequisite subgraph to be a DIRECTED ACYCLIC GRAPH. Because prereq is directed and asymmetric, the set of prereq edges must contain no cycle: a cycle would mean A must be learned before B AND B before A, an unsatisfiable learning order [ESTIMATE — design consequence, high confidence]. A DAG guarantees a topological ordering — at least one valid sequence in which every concept follows its prerequisites — which is exactly the KST surmise relation whose acyclic structure constrains the reachable knowledge states and the fringe of items to teach next (Doignon & Falmagne 1985) [FACT-source: contenteng kb_book_decomposition]. The prereq DAG, not the flat spine, is what a true adaptive learning-path selector traverses; part_of and related edges are excluded from this acyclicity requirement (only prereq must be a DAG).

included: prereq edges must form a DAG
topological order = valid learning sequence
the KST surmise-relation grounding via contenteng
excluded: the cycle detection/breaking procedure (its own node)

pros.claim: An acyclic prereq graph guarantees a valid learning order exists and can be computed
pros.example: topologically sorting concepts so no card is taught before its prerequisites

cons.claim: Real prerequisite knowledge sometimes has mutual dependencies that a strict DAG cannot represent without arbitrary edge removal
cons.example: two concepts that genuinely bootstrap each other forced into an artificial order

failure_modes: allowing a prereq cycle that makes learning order unsatisfiable
applying the acyclicity requirement to part_of/related where it does not belong
acceptance_tests: the prereq subgraph is required to be a DAG, topological order is identified as the valid learning sequence, the KST grounding is cited to contenteng, and only prereq (not part_of/related) is subject to acyclicity
revisit_triggers: a prereq cycle is detected

nodes.definition: Detect and break cycles in the prereq subgraph, since the DAG invariant is not self-enforcing. On every prereq-edge insert (or in the nightly integrity pass) run a cycle check — a DFS back-edge detection or a failed topological sort — and REJECT or flag any edge that closes a cycle rather than silently accepting it [ESTIMATE — standard graph algorithm + design policy, high confidence]. A detected cycle is a content error (usually a mis-directed or over-eager prereq claim): resolve it by dropping the weakest-evidence edge in the cycle, downgrading one prereq to a 'related' edge, or referring it to human review — never by leaving the cycle in place. The app forge/gate analogy is direct: the KB-forge gate itself rejects dependency cycles, so the same discipline applies to the concept prereq graph.

included: cycle detection on insert / in the integrity pass
reject-or-flag rather than accept
resolution by weakest-edge drop / downgrade / human review
excluded: the full integrity-invariant set (its own node)

pros.claim: Checking for cycles at insert time keeps the prereq DAG valid by construction instead of discovering breakage later
pros.example: rejecting a new prereq edge that would make A require B and B require A

cons.claim: Automatic edge-dropping to break a cycle can remove a correct prerequisite if the weakest-evidence heuristic misjudges
cons.example: dropping the true prereq and keeping the erroneous reverse edge because the wrong one had a source tag

failure_modes: accepting an edge that closes a cycle without checking
auto-dropping the correct edge when breaking a cycle
acceptance_tests: a cycle check runs on prereq insert / in the integrity pass, cycle-closing edges are rejected or flagged not accepted, and resolution is by weakest-edge drop, downgrade to related, or human review
revisit_triggers: cycles recur from the same source

base.update_signal: recurring cycles or a mis-drop changes the detection/breaking policy

nodes.definition: Structure the part_of edges as a containment hierarchy: because part_of is directed and transitive, the part_of subgraph forms a tree (or containment DAG) aggregating fine concepts into larger units, and any node's mastery/coverage can be ROLLED UP its part_of ancestors [ESTIMATE — design synthesis, high confidence]. This maps directly onto the app's blueprint aggregation: individual Concepts roll up into INBDE Foundation-Knowledge areas (inbde_fk 1-10) and Clinical-Content sections (inbde_cc_section DTP/OHM/PP), which is exactly how the mastery report averages bkt_p_mastery per FK area and CC section [FACT-source: APP_RECON section 4c, 3b stage 5]. The part_of hierarchy is therefore the structural backbone of the mastery roll-up, distinct from the prereq DAG that drives learning order — the two overlap on nodes but must not be conflated.

included: part_of as a transitive containment tree/DAG
mastery/coverage roll-up along part_of ancestors
the map onto INBDE FK areas and CC sections

pros.example: averaging concept mastery up to 'FK6 Pathology' via part_of containment

cons.example: an FK area expressible both as a part_of parent node and as an integer attribute, risking two sources of truth

failure_modes: conflating the part_of hierarchy with the prereq DAG

acceptance_tests: part_of is structured as a transitive containment tree/DAG with roll-up along ancestors and mapped onto the app's FK-area/CC-section aggregation, kept distinct from the prereq DAG

nodes.definition: Detect hub nodes by CENTRALITY. A hub is a node with high degree — many incident edges (prereq, part_of and related combined, or per-type) — computable directly from the edge table as a degree count, with betweenness or PageRank as richer optional measures [ESTIMATE — standard graph-theory centrality, to source-verify]. contenteng already anticipates hubs at the term-harvest stage, marking heavily-indexed terms as hub nodes [FACT-source: contenteng kb_book_decomposition]; the graph makes that explicit and quantitative. A hub is high-connectivity because many other concepts depend on, contain, or associate with it, so it is a structural signal the learner model and the viz layer both consume — but degree alone can also flag a mislabeled catch-all node, so a hub is a candidate for attention, not automatically a high-yield concept.

nodes.definition: Define the baseline alternative to a full graph: a FLAT ORDERED SPINE — concepts in a single linear sequence (chapter/unit order) that approximates prerequisites without explicit edges, contenteng's Option F [FACT-source: contenteng kb_book_decomposition]. The spine is cheap to author (order falls out of the book) and cheap to schedule against (walk the list), and for a linear curriculum it is often sufficient. Its structural limit is that a line cannot express branching or converging prerequisites, hubs, or alternative learning paths — everything is forced into one order even when the true structure is a graph. The spine is the honest default the system starts from and the fallback it can always degrade to; the question is when the graph earns its added cost.

nodes.definition: Collect the invariants that must always hold, so the graph is checkable in one integrity pass: (1) no dangling endpoints — every edge's src and dst reference existing Concept nodes; (2) nodes exist before edges reference them (creation ordering); (3) closed relation vocabulary — every edge type is in {prereq, related, part_of}; (4) prereq subgraph is acyclic (a DAG); (5) no duplicate or contradictory edges — a (src,type,dst) triple is unique and prereq(A,B) with prereq(B,A) is a contradiction to reject; (6) every edge carries provenance [ESTIMATE — design synthesis over the preceding nodes, high confidence]. conflict_axes.name: flat_spine_vs_full_graph
conflict_axes.description: A single linear ordering is cheap and always schedulable, but a branching prerequisite graph is required for real adaptive selection, hubs and roll-up.

conflict_axes.name: rich_proposition_vs_closed_typed_relation
conflict_axes.description: Concept-map propositions can express any relation in free text, but a queryable graph needs a small closed set of typed relations.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: author meaning as a proposition but persist a closed type; extend the vocabulary only by governed schema change

conflict_axes.name: closed_vocabulary_vs_expressive_relations
conflict_axes.description: A closed three-type vocabulary is checkable and reusable but cannot represent clinically real relations like treats/causes/contradicts.
poles: keep the vocabulary closed at three types
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: resist overloading 'related'; add a type only when a distinct relation is repeatedly needed and its algebra/invariants are defined

conflict_axes.name: directed_prereq_vs_symmetric_related
conflict_axes.description: prereq imposes an asymmetric learning order while related is symmetric; treating one as the other silently corrupts traversal.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: fix directionality per type as a schema property and traverse each type by its own algebra

conflict_axes.name: prereq_dag_strictness_vs_mutual_dependency
conflict_axes.description: Acyclicity guarantees a learning order but cannot represent genuinely mutually-bootstrapping concepts without dropping an edge.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep prereq acyclic and resolve a real mutual dependency by downgrading one edge to related or merging the concepts

conflict_axes.name: hub_centrality_vs_exam_yield
conflict_axes.description: Degree centrality flags well-connected nodes, which may or may not be the high-yield concepts the exam actually tests.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat hub centrality as one input to high-yield priority, cross-checked against exam-frequency, never as an automatic override

conflict_axes.name: eager_graph_vs_lazy_graduation
conflict_axes.description: Building the full graph early gives structure sooner but risks machinery no code consumes; deferring risks arriving with no captured edges.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: defer the live graph but capture edges continuously so materialization is cheap when a consumer arrives

conflict_axes.name: provenance_strictness_vs_population_speed
conflict_axes.description: Requiring a source on every edge keeps the graph honest but slows population, especially for cheap LLM-inferred edges.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: quarantine unsourced/LLM edges as candidates and promote them only on sourcing, so honesty gates speed

conflict_axes.name: part_of_edges_vs_attribute_aggregation

conflict_axes.resolution_hint: pick one source of aggregation truth per axis and derive the other from it rather than maintaining both independently

workflow.action: Map the schema onto Concept/ConceptEdge and attach provenance
workflow.description: Map nodes to Concept and edges to ConceptEdge, note the single reader and absent writer, and require edge provenance
workflow.gate: nodes/edges map to Concept/ConceptEdge, the one reader and missing writer are recorded, and provenance is required per edge

workflow.action: Enforce integrity invariants and issue the schema verdict
workflow.description: Run the six-invariant integrity pass and commit to the typed property graph with its graduation path and no-gos
workflow.gate: the six invariants are checked and the go/no-go verdict (typed property graph, prereq DAG + part_of + related + hubs; hybrid until a consumer; no free-text types, unsourced edges or cycles) is stated

dominance_rules.rule: A named consumer dominates aspiration in deciding whether to build the full graph
dominance_rules.rationale: the app reads ConceptEdge in one place and writes it nowhere, so a graph with no reader is premature complexity
dominance_rules.action: build the live graph only when adaptive selection, roll-up or hub priority will traverse it; otherwise keep the hybrid

dominance_rules.rule: Edge provenance dominates connectivity when admitting an edge
dominance_rules.rationale: a fabricated or unsourced prereq corrupts learning-path traversal with false authority
dominance_rules.trigger: an unsourced or LLM-inferred edge is about to be committed
dominance_rules.action: quarantine it as a candidate and promote only when a claim/source is attached

dominance_rules.rationale: a cycle makes the learning order unsatisfiable
dominance_rules.trigger: a new prereq edge would close a cycle
dominance_rules.action: reject or break the cycle by dropping the weakest-evidence edge or downgrading it to related

dominance_rules.rule: The closed relation vocabulary dominates ad-hoc relation labels
dominance_rules.rationale: free-text types defeat the per-type traversal and integrity checks
dominance_rules.trigger: a relation outside prereq/part_of/related is needed
dominance_rules.action: make a governed schema change with defined algebra and invariants, never a free-text label

dominance_rules.rule: Schema-level directionality dominates per-edge direction choices
dominance_rules.rationale: mixing prereq (asymmetric) and related (symmetric) corrupts traversal silently
dominance_rules.trigger: an edge type's direction is being set per edge
dominance_rules.action: fix direction and algebra as a property of the type and honor it in every traversal

dominance_rules.rule: Node existence dominates edge creation ordering
dominance_rules.rationale: a dangling edge references a node that is not there
dominance_rules.trigger: an edge is about to be written
dominance_rules.action: ensure both endpoint Concepts exist first, else reject the edge

dominance_rules.rule: One source of aggregation truth dominates dual maintenance
dominance_rules.rationale: part_of edges and inbde_fk attributes drift if both are authoritative
dominance_rules.trigger: aggregation is encoded both as edges and as attributes
dominance_rules.action: pick one source per axis and derive the other from it

dominance_rules.rule: Exam-yield cross-check dominates raw centrality for priority
dominance_rules.rationale: high connectivity is not the same as tested high-yield
dominance_rules.trigger: hub centrality is used to set study priority
dominance_rules.action: treat centrality as one signal cross-checked against exam frequency, not an automatic override

dominance_rules.rule: The flat spine dominates the full graph until a consumer justifies graduation
dominance_rules.rationale: the spine is cheaper and always schedulable and the graph adds invariant cost
dominance_rules.trigger: the graph is proposed to replace the spine
dominance_rules.action: keep the spine as the backbone, capture edges, and graduate only on demand

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix the entity-vs-relation split and the edge=proposition definition before designing any schema
anti_rework_rules.prevents: encoding relationships as node attributes and reworking the whole model

anti_rework_rules.rule: Adopt contenteng's proposition and vocabulary rather than defining new ones
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a graph edge incompatible with the flashcard edge that must later be reconciled

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set per-type directionality and the prereq-DAG requirement before writing any traversal
anti_rework_rules.prevents: traversals that follow prereq backward or miss transitive part_of ancestors

anti_rework_rules.rule: Enforce node-exists-before-edge from the first writer
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a graph full of dangling edges that must be swept later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Capture the lightweight edge table during the flat-spine phase
anti_rework_rules.prevents: retroactive edge extraction when a consumer finally needs the graph

anti_rework_rules.rule: Require edge provenance when the ConceptEdge writer is first built
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an unsourced/fabricated-edge cleanup after the graph is populated

anti_rework_rules.rule: Treat the (src,type,dst) triple as the edge identity and upsert
anti_rework_rules.prevents: duplicate edges accumulating across extraction runs

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose one source of aggregation truth (part_of edges vs inbde_fk attributes) up front
anti_rework_rules.prevents: divergent aggregation that must be reconciled across the mastery report

iteration_protocol.trigger: an adaptive-selection, mastery-roll-up or hub-priority consumer becomes real
iteration_protocol.action: materialize the live typed graph from the captured edges and re-run the integrity pass

iteration_protocol.trigger: a ConceptEdge writer is built in the app
iteration_protocol.action: wire node-exists, closed-vocabulary, acyclicity and provenance checks into the writer

iteration_protocol.trigger: a prereq cycle or a contradictory prereq pair is detected
iteration_protocol.action: break the cycle by weakest-edge drop or downgrade and record the resolution

iteration_protocol.trigger: a relation outside prereq/part_of/related is repeatedly needed
iteration_protocol.action: evaluate a governed vocabulary extension with its own directionality and invariants

iteration_protocol.trigger: hub centrality mis-ranks against measured exam yield
iteration_protocol.action: re-weight hub priority as one signal cross-checked with exam frequency

iteration_protocol.trigger: part_of edges and inbde_fk/cc_section attributes drift apart
iteration_protocol.action: pick one authoritative aggregation source and derive the other, adding a consistency check

iteration_protocol.trigger: the terminology-linking KB delivers synonym normalization
iteration_protocol.action: re-key node identity on canonical terms and merge duplicate nodes with their edges

priority_rationale: The problem frame and the entity-vs-relation split come first because they decide that meaning lives on typed edges and anchors on nodes; the edge-as-proposition grounding, the typed node and edge schemas, the property-graph choice and the relation vocabulary then fix what a node and an edge ARE; per-type directionality, the prerequisite DAG with its cycle detection, the part_of containment hierarchy and hub detection supply the structural layer; the flat-spine baseline, the demand-driven graduation trigger and the hybrid spine-plus-edges resolve when the graph earns its cost; and the app Concept/ConceptEdge mappings, edge provenance, the integrity invariants and the schema verdict come last because they bind the whole schema to the real entities and to an honest, checkable, consumer-gated commitment.
